judgments.reason: The lesson describes design data (net-lists/artwork) transferred between JPL and vendors using incompatible CAD tools, with conversion errors undetected because the interface was never verified — directly Part A; it says nothing about thruster small forces or trajectory.

The anomaly escaped because bench thermal testing of the integrated subsystem was deleted and prior subassembly tests were assumed adequate, matching the skipped-functional-test theme, but no inverted/backwards hardware is involved.

The root cause was a miswired harness with reversed 28V polarity, squarely Part A; the safe-to-mate test was incomplete but the lesson focuses on documentation/QA review shortcuts rather than a test replaced by inspection of an inherited design.
Describes a check valve spring installed backwards causing failure, a clear backwards-installation event, with the fix being an added inspection rather than a skipped-test lesson.
The failure stemmed from erroneously assuming an inherited design was acceptable without re-analysis under new environments, matching the untested-heritage aspect of Part B.
A circuit design error escaped reviews, but the tests were performed (they just validated the erroneous design); no reversed orientation and no skipped test or heritage trust.
Generic recommendation to perform end-to-end functional verification for safety-critical hardware, not an account of a test being replaced by inspection or an inverted part.
Directly about heritage designs carried over and not requalified for the new mission, the inherited-design-trusted-without-re-verification element of Part B.
Inherited TDRS antenna design was reused for a different mission and inheritance/design reviews failed to catch the flaw, illustrating trusting heritage without adequate re-verification.

The pyro electronics fault escaped because ground support equipment lacked fidelity and no as-flown end-to-end test existed, but it is a design transient issue, not an inverted part nor a test replaced by inspection/heritage trust.
Describes a digital logic transient design error causing premature pyro firing; no reversed orientation and no skipped test substituted by inspection or inherited design.
Touchdown sensor wiring errors (Part A) plus the failure to rerun the full leg deployment test after rewiring, letting the flaw escape (Part B).

The TOPEX/POSEIDON overturning incident stemmed from an unstable lifting fixture/spreader bar design, not from an undocumented hardware configuration change or a failure to verify configuration before moving.

Six attachment bolts were removed from the SRM lifting bracket without work authorization or traceability, and the segment was hoisted, mated and moved before anyone discovered the missing hardware, with recommendations to add inspections of transferred support equipment.

The trunnion covers were modified late in the flow with the part-number/tether change not communicated to checklists or mockups, matching uncommunicated hardware configuration change, but the lesson is not about a crew failing to verify configuration before operating.

Maintenance left the filter cover secured by only three of sixteen bolts with no record, and the test crew pressurized the system without any check of assembly completion, exactly matching both parts.
This near-drop lesson concerns reuse and stability analysis of an inherited lifting fixture, not an unrecorded configuration change or an unverified pre-move configuration check.

The wind tunnel model failed because required fasteners were never installed and repeated inspections missed them; it is a workmanship/inspection-quality lesson rather than an unrecorded configuration change handed off between teams.

The EMU drop resulted from using the ground test fixture outside its certified 4-pin design with no procedure for its use, not from hardware left altered by a prior team or an omitted configuration verification.

A GSE fitting was removed and reinstalled without torqueing or leak check (and a filter left unmaintained), and testing proceeded with no procedure to verify the GSE configuration/leak status before use, leading to the burst disc and overpressure failures.

The lesson is precisely that an onboard safing sequence was not constrained to the proper mission phase and enabled/fired thrusters on the pad, matching Part B, but the triggering event was an inadvertently issued stored command rather than a false/transient sensor signal.

WIRE's loss was caused by power-up transients/non-deterministic logic states (Part A) that the pyro box control logic acted upon because the design failed to inhibit or account for those transients (Part B).
